summary: In Greek mythology, Perseus is the legendary founder of the Perseid dynasty and, with Cadmus and Bellerophon, among the greatest Greek heroes and monster-slayers before Heracles. Son of Zeus and Danaë, he beheaded the Gorgon Medusa for King Polydectes of Seriphos and rescued Andromeda from the sea monster Cetus. He became an ancestor of Heracles and was credited with founding or fortifying Mycenae.
etymology: The name Perseus is often thought pre-Greek, though a Greek derivation from pérthein ("to waste, ravage, sack") with the agent suffix -eus yields "sacker [of cities]," a fitting name for an early warrior hero. A folk etymology connected him with the Persians (Pérsai) through his son Perses; Herodotus reports that Xerxes tried to exploit this kinship with Argos.

sections.heading: Birth and Seriphos
paragraphs: King Acrisius of Argos, warned by Delphi that his grandson would kill him, locked his daughter Danaë in a bronze chamber. Zeus visited her as a shower of gold, and she bore Perseus. Unwilling to kill Zeus's child, Acrisius cast mother and infant to sea in a chest; they washed ashore on Seriphos, where the fisherman Dictys raised the boy. Dictys's brother Polydectes, king of the island, later lusted after Danaë and sought to remove Perseus by demanding Medusa's head as a gift.

sections.heading: Medusa and Andromeda
paragraphs: Hermes and Athena armed Perseus with winged sandals, a harpe, Hades's helm of invisibility, a kibisis for the head, and a polished shield in which to view Medusa safely. After forcing the Graeae to reveal the Gorgons' lair, he beheaded the mortal Medusa while she slept; from her neck sprang Pegasus and Chrysaor. Returning, he used the still-potent head to petrify foes, including — in some tellings — Atlas.

In Aethiopia he found Andromeda chained as a sacrifice to Cetus after her mother Cassiopeia's boast offended the Nereids. Perseus slew the monster, married Andromeda despite her betrothed Phineus (whom he petrified), and on Seriphos turned Polydectes to stone, making Dictys king. He gave Medusa's head to Athena for her aegis.

sections.heading: Prophecy, Mycenae, and descendants
paragraphs: The oracle was fulfilled when Perseus accidentally killed Acrisius with a discus or quoit at games in Larissa. Ashamed to take Argos by bloodshed, he exchanged kingdoms with Megapenthes and ruled from Tiryns; Pausanias and others credit him with founding or fortifying Mycenae. With Andromeda he fathered Perses (left as ancestor of the Persians in Greek lore), Alcaeus, Electryon, Sthenelus, Gorgophone, and others — the Perseid line that leads to Alcmene and Heracles.

Greek tradition treated Perseus as a quasi-historical figure; Pausanias notes a roadside shrine between Mycenae and Argos and a sacred fountain Persea at Mycenae. The hero and Andromeda were also placed among the constellations.
